notes: This is the largest and most complex of the assigned owners (404 bytes, 7 saved registers, 6 literal-pool constants, ~15 calls, a genuine input-polling menu loop). The template (Menu_RunSelection) is only a loose structural cousin -- both build one or more objects then poll an input-flag loop -- but this owner's actual logic, read from games/gs1/asm/0802977c.s, is materially different: it creates a background window (Func_08019da8) and a second UI object (Func_080162d4), counts entries in TWO separate -1-terminated tables at fixed addresses 0x080367e4 and 0x0803680c (4-byte stride, value at +2) to get two sub-list lengths and their sum, then loops reading an input-flags word from *0x03001b04 to adjust a selection index (up/down/left/right bit tests each moving the index by 1 or 10, with independent `str [sp,#8]` dirty-flag sets per direction rather than a single combined OR), exits on two different confirm/cancel bit masks (0x1 or a `r9`-held mask of 2, not spelled out as a literal 2 in every branch the way I assumed), and otherwise re-clamps the index via Func_080022fc, repositions the highlighted row via Func_08016478/Func_0801a4fc/Func_0801ea08/Func_0801e7c0 using whichever of the two tables the clamped index falls into, before looping again on Func_080030f8(1).

One direct-translation pass was written and measured (candidate 356B vs reference 404B, wrong_instructions=168 -- i.e. the overall shape and byte count are both off by a wide margin, not just register-numbering noise). This reflects a first-pass reading of the assembly under this batch's per-owner effort budget, not a converged or even close attempt; I did not iterate given how far off the very first measurement already was and the number of remaining assigned owners.

Known inaccuracies in the current draft, in order of how much I expect they matter: (1) the four directional key checks in the real assembly each independently `str 1,[sp,#8]` a dirty flag AND adjust `r5` (candidate treats this as `flag=1; index+=/-=N` per direction, which is probably right but the exact bit values 0x20/0x10/0x200/0x100 are read directly from the assembly's mask constants -- movs 32, movs 16, 128<<2=512, 128<<1=256 -- so those four are higher-confidence); (2) the exit condition in the real code is `(keys & 1) != 0 THEN check .L8` OR `(keys & r9) != 0 THEN check .L8` where r9 is a runtime value initialized to 2 that is never reassigned in this function -- I collapsed r9 to the literal 2 in the candidate, which is probably correct but unverified; (3) the real code reloads `Data_03001b04`'s underlying flags word (via `ldr r3,[r6,#0]`) SEPARATELY for each of the six bit tests rather than caching it once into a `keys` local the way the candidate does, which alone likely accounts for a large share of the instruction-count gap; (4) the table-lookup stride/offset (index*4+2) and the y+128 adjustment for the second table are read from the assembly's `lsls r3,r5,#2; adds r3,#2` pattern and are reasonably confident, but the two tables' actual element types/counts are unconfirmed.

Given the size of the remaining gap, the most useful next step is a fresh pass that (a) does NOT cache Data_03001b04 into a local and instead re-reads the volatile flags word for every bit test exactly as the assembly does, and (b) treats the `r9`-held exit mask and the sp8 dirty-flag as literal per-branch stores rather than folding them into higher-level C control flow, before any permuter-style search is worthwhile.
